title: Massive (life-threatening) haemoptysis (adult)
subject: respiratory
summary: The threat is asphyxia, not blood loss: protect the airway, lie the patient bleeding side down, intubate early with a large tube, reverse anticoagulation, give tranexamic acid as a bridge, obtain CT angiography when stable, and arrange bronchial artery embolisation as first-line definitive control.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Life-threatening haemoptysis: more than 150 mL in 24 hours or 100 mL/hour, or any volume causing airway obstruction, respiratory failure or haemodynamic instability (SCII 2023). About 150 mL of blood can fill the tracheobronchial dead space, so poor cough or low reserve makes small volumes lethal.
Confirm the source: exclude haematemesis and nasopharyngeal bleeding.

In India TB accounts for most cases (65 to 79%): active TB, post-TB bronchiectasis, aspergilloma in an old cavity, and Rasmussen pulmonary artery pseudoaneurysm. Others: bronchiectasis, lung cancer, fungal infection, AV malformation, mitral stenosis, anticoagulants or coagulopathy.
Over 90% of massive bleeds arise from the high-pressure systemic (bronchial and non-bronchial) arteries, which is why embolisation works.

sections.title: Immediate management
items: Call for help early: airway expert, pulmonologist, interventional radiologist, intensivist, thoracic surgeon. Two working suction units, oxygen, two large-bore IV cannulae, crossmatch.
If the bleeding side is known, lie the patient in the lateral decubitus position with the bleeding lung down to protect the other lung.

Intubate early if the airway is threatened, cough is weak or reserve is poor: rapid sequence induction with an endotracheal tube of 8.0 mm or larger (8.5 mm or more preferred) to allow therapeutic bronchoscopy; suction-assisted laryngoscopy helps. Double-lumen tubes are generally discouraged.
Continued bleeding after intubation: advance the tube into the main bronchus of the non-bleeding lung (bronchoscope or bougie guided) or place a bronchial blocker.

Stop anticoagulants and antiplatelets. Warfarin: prothrombin complex concentrate 25 to 50 units/kg IV plus vitamin K 10 mg IV. Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV. Heparin: protamine. Factor Xa inhibitors: andexanet alfa where available.
Transfuse to haemoglobin above 7 g/dL, platelets above 50 x 10^9/L, INR below 1.5 and fibrinogen above 1.0 g/L.
Tranexamic acid as a bridge to definitive therapy: 1 g IV, then 500 mg to 1 g IV every 6 to 8 hours, or nebulised 500 mg in 5 mL saline every 8 hours. Reduce the IV dose in renal impairment.

sections.title: Investigations
items: CBC, coagulation profile, group and crossmatch, renal function, blood gas; chest X-ray to lateralise.

Multidetector CT angiography (neck to L2, arterial phase) is the investigation of choice once the patient is stable enough to travel: it localises the bleeding site, shows the cause, and maps bronchial, non-bronchial systemic and pulmonary arteries before embolisation.
Bronchoscopy localises the bleeding side, clears clot and guides tube placement; rigid bronchoscopy gives airway control and access for tamponade in massive bleeding.
Sputum AFB smear and NAAT (CBNAAT or Truenat) for TB; Aspergillus IgG if a cavity or fungal ball is present; echocardiography if mitral stenosis or pulmonary hypertension is suspected.

sections.title: Definitive control
items: Bronchial artery embolisation (BAE) is the first-line definitive treatment for life-threatening haemoptysis once stabilised (SCII 2023): technical success 81 to 100%, recurrence 9.8 to 57.5%. Early BAE is also advised for non-life-threatening haemoptysis with hypertrophied arteries on CT angiography.
Rasmussen aneurysm (pulmonary artery pseudoaneurysm in cavitary TB) needs pulmonary artery embolisation with coils or plugs; bronchial embolisation alone will not stop it.

Bronchoscopic temporising measures: cold saline (4 C) in 10 to 20 mL aliquots, topical adrenaline (10 mcg diluted in 10 mL saline aliquots), endobronchial tranexamic acid, balloon tamponade, bronchial blockers or thermal coagulation.

Surgery for failed embolisation or bronchoscopic control, localised disease with high recurrence risk (e.g. aspergilloma) or need for tissue diagnosis. Elective surgery after control has better outcomes than emergency resection.
Treat the cause: anti-TB treatment for confirmed active TB, antibiotics for bronchiectasis exacerbation, oncology referral for tumour.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Manage in ICU with continuous SpO2 and ECG, measured haemoptysis volumes, serial haemoglobin and coagulation.
After BAE watch for spinal cord ischaemia (0.2 to 6.5%: new leg weakness or sensory loss), chest pain, dysphagia and post-embolisation syndrome (usually self-limiting).
Recurrence is common, especially with aspergilloma, non-bronchial collaterals and cystic fibrosis; plan follow-up and definitive treatment of the cause.

sections.title: Escalate and transfer
items: All life-threatening haemoptysis belongs in ICU with a multidisciplinary team.
If interventional radiology is not available, secure the airway first, then transfer to a centre that can perform BAE.
Refractory bleeding despite BAE and bronchoscopic measures: urgent thoracic surgical review.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Judging severity by volume alone in a patient with poor lung reserve.
Sending an unprotected, actively bleeding patient to CT.
Intubating with a small tube that cannot pass a therapeutic bronchoscope.
Treating tranexamic acid as definitive therapy and delaying embolisation; missing a Rasmussen aneurysm or non-bronchial systemic collaterals.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid (IV)
drugs.dose: 1 g IV, then 500 mg to 1 g IV every 6 to 8 hours
drugs.notes: Bridge only. Reduce dose in renal impairment; caution with previous thromboembolism.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid (nebulised)
drugs.dose: 500 mg in 5 mL 0.9% saline nebulised every 8 hours, for up to 5 days
drugs.notes: Evidence mainly in non-massive haemoptysis; may cause bronchospasm.
